practice.stem: According to the lecture, the success of a pathogen (pathogenicity) depends on which three things?
options: Communicability, infectivity and virulence
Colonization, normal flora and portal of entry
Incubation, prodrome and acute illness
Toxigenicity, adhesion and evasion
practice.rationale: Slide 3: pathogenicity "depends on communicability, infectivity, and virulence" — C → I → V = P. "Know this process in general." Toxigenicity, adhesion and evasion are virulence factors (FYI list); incubation → acute are disease-course stages.

practice.stem: Virulence is best defined as the ability of an agent to:
options: Trigger any immune response at all
Cause severe disease or death
Invade the host and multiply there
Spread from one person to others
practice.rationale: Virulence = severity: the proportion of sick people who become severely ill or die (rabies high, the cold low). Spreading is communicability, invading and multiplying is infectivity, and inducing an immune response is immunogenicity.

practice.stem: Immunogenicity refers to:
options: The ability to induce an immune response
The ability to produce toxins
The ability to hide from immune cells
The ability to stick to and enter the body
practice.rationale: "The other term I want you to know from here is immunogenicity" — the ability to induce an immune response. Toxin production, adhesion and evasion are the other virulence factors on slide 4, which he said not to memorize.

practice.stem: Which statement describes an antigen?
options: A Y-shaped protein made by plasma cells
A protein that makes other proteins misfold and clump
Any substance the immune system recognizes
A receptor found only on T cells
practice.rationale: "Antigen, all it means is any substance that the immune system recognizes" — a toxin, a microbe's surface, a transplanted organ. The Y-shaped protein is the antibody; a misfolding protein is a prion.

practice.stem: Normal gut and skin flora living on a person without causing damage is an example of:
options: Subclinical disease
Infection
Bacteremia
Colonization
practice.rationale: Colonization = establishing a presence without damage — commensal flora that, "if anything, prevent disease." Infection means invasion that causes disease; bacteremia is bacteria in the blood; subclinical disease still involves some injury.

practice.stem: When are bacterial endotoxins released?
options: Only from gram-positive bacteria
When the bacteria are attacked and lysed
Constantly, as the bacteria grow and divide
Only after an antitoxin has bound them
practice.rationale: "Endo" = inside: endotoxins (LPS of gram-negative bacteria) come out only when bacteria are attacked and popped open — and then they hurt the immune cells that killed them. Constant release during growth is exotoxins ("exo" = exit).

practice.stem: On a Gram stain, gram-negative bacteria appear ___ and are generally ___.
options: Purple; harder for immune cells and antibiotics
Pink; harder for immune cells and antibiotics
Pink; more sensitive to antibiotics
Purple; more sensitive to antibiotics
practice.rationale: "Pink is negative, purple is positive." Gram-negative bacteria have an extra layer that helps them evade the immune system and antibiotics — "the armored tanks of the bacterial world." Gram-positive is the one more receptive to antibiotics.

practice.stem: Which describes a prion?
options: A bacterium that has no cell wall and no nucleus
A virus particle made of a protein coat around an RNA core
A misfolded protein that makes normal proteins misfold
A parasite carried by a mosquito vector
practice.rationale: Prions have no genome — they are abnormally shaped versions of your own proteins that make normal proteins misfold, clump and kill cells (mad cow disease). A protein coat around a nucleic-acid core is a virus.

practice.stem: Antibiotics inhibit bacteria by inhibiting all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Nucleic-acid synthesis in bacteria
Bacterial cell-wall synthesis
Bacterial protein synthesis
Ergosterol in the cell membrane
practice.rationale: Slide 17's antibiotic targets: cell-wall synthesis, protein synthesis, nucleic-acid synthesis and metabolism. Ergosterol in the membrane is an antifungal target (slide 19) — and antibiotics will not kill fungi.

practice.stem: Which is a way bacteria "fight back" against antibiotics?
options: Increasing the number of binding sites for the drug
Making new protein coats (capsids)
Altering the antibiotic's binding site
Building more ergosterol in the wall
practice.rationale: Slide 17: bacteria fight back by inactivating antibiotics, altering antibiotic binding sites, using different metabolic pathways and changing their cell walls to keep the drug out. Capsids are viral; ergosterol is fungal.

practice.stem: Antifungal drugs inhibit fungi by targeting:
options: Peptidoglycan cross-links in the fungal cell wall
Enzymes that build new capsids, or protein coats
Ergosterol in the membrane and glucan in the wall
Protein synthesis at the fungal ribosome
practice.rationale: Slide 19: antifungals inhibit ergosterol in fungal cell membranes and glucan in fungal cell walls. The fungal wall is polysaccharide, not peptidoglycan, which is why antibiotics won't kill fungi. Capsid-building enzymes are antiviral targets, and protein synthesis is an antibiotic target in bacteria.

practice.stem: Where do B cells and T cells undergo selection?
options: B cells in the thymus; T cells in the bone marrow
Both in the spleen
B cells in the bone marrow; T cells in the thymus
Both in the lymph nodes
practice.rationale: "For B cells, the selection process happens in the bone marrow. You need to know that. For T cells … the thymus." Both are produced in the bone marrow; afterwards both go to the lymph nodes to wait.

practice.stem: During negative selection, a developing lymphocyte is told to die when it:
options: Binds to nothing at all
Binds self-antigens too strongly
Fails to divide fast enough
Binds only weakly to a foreign antigen
practice.rationale: Negative selection removes cells that bind self too hard — "that's how you prevent autoimmune diseases." Cells that bind nothing are removed earlier, in positive selection, because they're useless. Together = tolerance.

practice.stem: Antigen-presenting cells show antigen to T cells on which molecule?
options: The B-cell receptor
MHC class II
IgE
MHC class I
practice.rationale: "Just remember, it's MHC class II" (HLA antigens in humans) on dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. MHC I is also on cells and matters in transplant matching, but it isn't the APC answer he drilled; IgE is the type I antibody.

practice.stem: Which antibody function is "direct" — carried out by the antibody alone?
options: Complement activation
Agglutination
Inflammation
Phagocytosis
practice.rationale: Slide 38: direct functions are neutralization, agglutination (clumping cells) and precipitation (soluble antigens). Inflammation, phagocytosis and complement are indirect — they need other components.

practice.stem: Which statement about second-generation H1 antagonists is correct?
options: They work by stopping mast cells from releasing histamine
They have strong atropine-like anticholinergic effects
They are the highly sedating group, like diphenhydramine
They cross the blood-brain barrier poorly and sedate much less
practice.rationale: Second generation (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) cross the BBB poorly, have low affinity for CNS H1 receptors and are largely devoid of anticholinergic action. Diphenhydramine is first generation. No antihistamine stops mast-cell release — they only block the receptor.

practice.stem: A client with measles coughed in an exam room and left. Why is the next client who enters an hour later at risk?
options: Measles is a prion disease that survives cleaning
Measles is highly virulent, so any exposure is fatal
Measles is highly communicable — it stays in the air for hours
Measles spreads mainly by touching the exam table and the chair
practice.rationale: Measles is the slide's example of high communicability: the virus can linger in a room up to 8–10 hours and spreads through the air. Communicability (spread) isn't the same as virulence (severity); measles is a virus, not a prion.

practice.stem: A client reports fever, muscle aches, headache and fatigue, plus diarrhea since yesterday. Which finding is a local (specific) sign?
options: Myalgia
Headache
Fever
Diarrhea
practice.rationale: Diarrhea points to the site — the GI tract. Fever, myalgia, headache and lethargy are systemic/nonspecific. The headache is systemic because it comes from vasodilation and whole-body inflammation; "your brain has no sensory" receptors.

practice.stem: A student had a scratchy throat after her roommate's flu, felt fine the next morning, and never got sick. This is best described as:
options: Subclinical disease
Chronic disease
The prodromal stage
The convalescent stage
practice.rationale: His exact example: the immune system cleared it below the clinical threshold — subclinical disease, with little to no signs or symptoms. Prodrome is the start of real symptoms on the way to acute illness; convalescence follows an acute illness.

practice.stem: Why is tuberculosis the classic example of chronic disease on the disease-course curve?
options: It always progresses past the critical threshold
It is cleared within days by the innate system
It never causes symptoms, so it always stays below the clinical threshold
The immune system walls it off in the lung but can't clear it
practice.rationale: TB grows slowly and defends itself, so the immune system walls it off — "not 100% secure," and it can break out again. That's the chronic branch: kept at bay, not cleared. Staying below the threshold is subclinical; passing the critical threshold is death.

practice.stem: A client with a foot infection has a tender, swollen lymph node behind the knee. The nurse understands this means:
options: Lymphocytes are proliferating there, and an infection is active
The innate immune system has failed completely
The client has a primary immunodeficiency
Bacteria have spread from the foot and are now growing inside the node
practice.rationale: Swollen nodes mean T and B cells are dividing — "a bad, good thing": the immune system is working, but there is an active infection. APCs go to the closest node, so a foot infection shows up behind the knee.

practice.stem: A father fully vaccinated against pertussis carries the bacteria after a work exposure. Why can he still give his unvaccinated infant whooping cough?
options: Vaccinated adults don't form memory cells against pertussis at all
Pertussis vaccines wear off within a few days
The vaccine targets the toxin, so bacteria can still grow and spread
The bacteria mutate too quickly for any pertussis vaccine to keep up
practice.rationale: The pertussis vaccine is against the toxin, not the bacteria. He neutralizes the toxin, but the bacteria still grow and can be passed to someone unvaccinated, who then makes the toxin and gets whooping cough. That is why high vaccination rates matter.

practice.stem: A new mother asks how her newborn is protected before the baby has made its own T- and B-cell repertoire. The nurse explains:
options: The newborn's thymus has already finished selecting a full repertoire
Antibodies in breast milk, plus vaccinated parents around the baby
Newborn stomach acid destroys pathogens
Newborns are born with a full set of memory T and B cells from the mother
practice.rationale: "Breast milk" — its antibodies can cross into the infant's bloodstream because infant stomachs aren't very acidic yet; parents should be vaccinated. The repertoire builds slowly after birth, so infants aren't born with memory cells.

practice.stem: A client says, "My last bee sting was no big deal, so I can't be allergic." Which response reflects the lecture?
options: "If you were going to be allergic, you'd have reacted the very first time."
"The first sting can sensitize you, so the next one may cause a reaction."
"Bee allergy is inherited, so one sting doesn't change anything."
"Each sting makes a reaction less likely as you build tolerance."
practice.rationale: You can only react to what your immune system has seen. The first sting is the sensitizing event: T and B cells take 7–14 days, the venom is long gone, so no reaction. Next time there may be one, and "the more bee stings you have," the higher the chance.

practice.stem: An 82-year-old client takes diphenhydramine (Benadryl) nightly for sleep. Which effect is the nurse most concerned about?
options: Paradoxical hyperactivity and rebound insomnia
Low blood glucose
Increased milk production
Confusion, urinary retention and falls
practice.rationale: Older adults are on the caution list: serious anticholinergic effects (confusion, sedation, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention), more falls and a possible dementia link. Paradoxical hyperactivity is the young-child warning; decreased milk is the nursing-mother warning.

practice.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is started on pyridostigmine. How does this drug help?
options: It removes the receptor-blocking antibodies from her blood
It slows the breakdown of acetylcholine, so more is available
It blocks histamine at the neuromuscular junction so muscles relax
It removes the thymus's extra T cells
practice.rationale: Antibodies block the ACh receptors, so pyridostigmine (an AChE inhibitor) keeps more ACh around — "increase the amount of acetylcholine by stopping its breakdown." Removing antibodies is plasma exchange; removing the thymus is thymectomy.

practice.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis is admitted in myasthenic crisis. Which treatments does the slide list for crisis?
options: Second-generation antihistamines
Plasma exchange and IV immune globulin
Hydroxychloroquine and NSAIDs
Rho(D) immune globulin IM
practice.rationale: Slide 68: "plasma exchange and intravenous immune globulin should be given in myasthenic crises" — plasma exchange cleans antibodies out of the blood. Hydroxychloroquine and NSAIDs are on the SLE slide; Rho(D) immune globulin is for Rh sensitization.

practice.stem: Ten days after receiving antivenom for a rattlesnake bite, a client has fever, rash, swollen lymph nodes and painful joints. The nurse recognizes:
options: Graft-versus-host disease
A delayed type I reaction to venom left in the tissues
A delayed type IV skin reaction
Serum sickness from circulating immune complexes
practice.rationale: Antivenom is the classic trigger of serum sickness (type III): antibody–antigen complexes get stuck in blood vessels, joints and kidneys → fever, enlarged nodes, rash, pain, arthritis. Type I is immediate and IgE-driven; GVHD follows bone marrow transplant.

practice.stem: An Rh-negative woman just delivered her first Rh-positive baby. Which statement is accurate?
options: Sensitization is prevented by giving the baby antihistamines
Birth can sensitize her, so a future Rh-positive baby is at risk
The risk only applies if the father is Rh-negative
This baby was at highest risk because it was the first pregnancy
practice.rationale: The first baby is usually fine because there was no sensitizing event; birth is the sensitizing event, and the problem is the second Rh-positive baby (hemolytic disease of the newborn). Slide 78 lists Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM), given IM.

practice.stem: A client receiving a kidney from her brother asks if she'll need immunosuppressants. The nurse's answer is based on the fact that:
options: A negative crossmatch before surgery means that acute or chronic rejection can no longer occur
Even close-family grafts usually need them lifelong; identical twins are the exception
Immunosuppressants are needed only for the first month, until the graft heals
A brother is a perfect HLA match, so she won't have any rejection at all
practice.rationale: Even matching well, most people develop acute or chronic (type IV) rejection, so "even if it's from a close family member… immunosuppressants the rest of your life." Identical twins are the exception. A negative crossmatch prevents hyperacute (type II) rejection only.

practice.stem: A client has fever, muscle aches and fatigue the day after an mRNA vaccine. According to the vaccination deck, these effects come from:
options: Memory T cells attacking the muscle cells that took up the mRNA
A type I allergic reaction to the mRNA
The innate inflammatory/immune response to the vaccine
A mild case of the infection caused by the vaccine
practice.rationale: V-slide 5: the innate inflammatory/immune response causes the side effects seen 24–48 hours after vaccination — lethargy, myalgia, fever, headache. mRNA is very immunogenic. The vaccine doesn't cause the infection, and this isn't an allergy.

practice.stem: A client vaccinated in the left deltoid has a tender lump in the left armpit three days later. The best explanation is:
options: APCs carried the antigen to the closest lymph node, where T cells are proliferating
Vaccine fluid leaked down from the deltoid and formed a small abscess in the armpit
The client has a primary immunodeficiency
Antibodies made against the vaccine are now attacking the client's own lymph tissue
practice.rationale: V-slide 6: APCs travel to the closest lymph node — a shoulder shot means the armpit node. A matching T cell binds and proliferates there, and proliferation is what makes a node swell.

practice.stem: A client's leg abscess hasn't improved after a week of IV antibiotics, and imaging shows a biofilm. Which intervention does the lecture list?
options: A switch to an antifungal
An antihistamine to reduce the swelling
Stopping all antibiotics to rebuild natural immunity
Surgical drainage and debridement
practice.rationale: Slide 20: surgical interventions — remove infected tissue, drain abscesses, debridement — for when antibiotics aren't reaching bacteria in a thick biofilm. An antifungal won't treat bacteria, and "natural immunity" means you run the risk of dying.

practice.stem: Hives, itching and wheezing within minutes of eating peanuts, after previous exposure. Hypersensitivity type?
options: Type III
Type II
Type IV
Type I
practice.rationale: Immediate reaction to an exogenous allergen through IgE on mast cells → histamine = type I (allergy). Type IV would take 24–72 h; types II and III involve IgG/IgM against tissue or immune complexes.

practice.stem: A red, itchy, blistering rash appears 2 days after the client cleared poison ivy from a fence. Hypersensitivity type?
options: Type IV
Type III
Type I
Type II
practice.rationale: Poison ivy is on the type IV list: sensitized T cells have to travel to the site, so it's delayed — 24–72 hours. Type I is immediate.

practice.stem: Minutes into a transfusion of the wrong ABO type, the client's red cells are being destroyed. Classify the reaction.
options: Type IV alloimmunity
Type II alloimmunity
Type III autoimmunity
Type I allergy
practice.rationale: Reaction to another person's tissue = alloimmunity; the slides put ABO transfusion reactions under type II (antibodies against the A/B antigens on the donor cells).

practice.stem: SLE: autoantibodies to histones and nucleic acids form circulating complexes that deposit in kidneys and joints. Classify it.
options: Type IV autoimmunity
Type III alloimmunity
Type III autoimmunity
Type II autoimmunity
practice.rationale: Self antigens = autoimmunity; circulating immune complexes that deposit = type III (slide 74 says so outright). Type II binds a specific tissue rather than circulating; there's no other person's tissue here, so it isn't alloimmunity.

practice.stem: A child develops local swelling and tissue necrosis at a vaccine injection site from antibody–antigen complexes. Which reaction is this?
options: Serum sickness (type III, systemic)
Anaphylaxis (type I, systemic)
Arthus reaction (type III, local)
Graft rejection (type IV)
practice.rationale: Type III can be hyper-local: the Arthus reaction. A child already exposed has antibodies ready, which meet the concentrated antigen at the injection site. Serum sickness is the systemic version (antivenom).

practice.stem: Three days after a booster, a client's antibody level against the vaccine antigen has already risen sharply. Which response is this?
options: Primary immune response
Innate immune response
Secondary immune response
Type I hypersensitivity
practice.rationale: Boosters cause a secondary response: memory B cells respond immediately, and antibody levels rise within days. A primary response (first vaccination) takes 2–3 weeks.

practice.stem: An infant has had repeated severe infections since birth and makes no functional B or T cells. Classify the deficiency.
options: Primary — combined (SCID)
Acquired — malnutrition
Acquired — AIDS
Primary — complement (C3)
practice.rationale: Never producing B and T cells is severe combined immunodeficiency — a primary (congenital/genetic) defect, "your bubble boy." Acquired deficiencies come from another condition; C3 deficiency is complement.

practice.stem: A client with alcoholic cirrhosis gets frequent infections. Classify the immune problem.
options: Primary — phagocyte defect
Hypersensitivity — type III immune complexes
Primary — B-cell defect
Acquired — reduced complement
practice.rationale: Alcoholic cirrhosis is on the acquired list; he added, "that's a decrease in your complement." The immune system itself is fine — another illness impairs it. A primary deficiency is congenital.

practice.stem: A client has recurrent pneumonia and granulomas because phagocytes can't kill what they engulf (myeloperoxidase–H₂O₂ defect). Classify it.
options: Primary — B-cell (hypogammaglobulinemia)
Acquired — burns
Primary — innate (mucocutaneous candidiasis)
Primary — phagocyte (chronic granulomatous disease)
practice.rationale: Chronic granulomatous disease is a primary phagocyte deficiency: a defect in the myeloperoxidase–hydrogen peroxide system means phagocytes can't kill, giving recurrent pneumonia and tumor-like granulomas. Mucocutaneous candidiasis is recurrent Candida.

practice.stem: Within minutes of reperfusion, a transplanted kidney fails because the recipient already had antibodies to graft antigens. Classify it.
options: Hyperacute rejection — type II
Chronic rejection — type IV
Graft-versus-host disease — type IV
Acute rejection — type IV
practice.rationale: Immediate rejection from preexisting antibody = hyperacute (type II), the one crossmatching prevents. Acute (days–months) and chronic (months–years) are cell-mediated, type IV.

practice.stem: Six weeks after a kidney transplant, T cells attack unmatched HLA antigens on the graft. Classify it.
options: Serum sickness — type III
Acute rejection — type IV
Chronic rejection — type III
Hyperacute rejection — type II
practice.rationale: Days to months, cell-mediated against unmatched HLA = acute rejection, type IV. Chronic rejection (months–years, minor HLA) is also type IV, not III; hyperacute is immediate and antibody-mediated.

practice.stem: Step-by-step: an APC has just presented strep antigen on MHC II at the throat. What happens next?
options: Memory T and B cells form
B cells turn into plasma cells
The APC travels to the closest lymph tissue
T cells recruit macrophages and cytotoxic T cells to the throat
practice.rationale: Step 4 (present on MHC II) → step 5: APCs travel to the closest lymph tissue → 6 the right T cell binds → 7 clonal proliferation → 8 T cells leave, plasma cells make antibodies → 9–10 find the site, recruit effectors → 11 memory.

clinical.title: Scenario 1 — Medical-surgical unit
clinical.setting: Infected abdominal wound with septicemia · days 1–4
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1400 64-year-old client, post-op day 6 after bowel surgery. Reports chills, aching muscles, a headache and feeling "wiped out." The lower end of the incision is red and swollen, with a fluctuant pocket draining cloudy fluid. History of type 2 diabetes. Ambulating in the hall twice a day. Wife visits every afternoon. Vital Signs — T 39.1°C · HR 112 · BP 98/60 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 96% on room air Laboratory Results — Blood cultures ×2 and wound culture: collected 1330, pending Orders — IV antibiotic · surgical consult for the wound · vital signs every 2 h

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the nurses' notes. Which findings are systemic (nonspecific) signs of infection? Select all that apply.
options: Cloudy wound drainage
Headache
Aching muscles
Temperature 39.1°C
Red, swollen lower incision
Feeling "wiped out"
questions.rationale: Fever, myalgia, headache and lethargy are the slide's systemic/nonspecific signs. The headache counts as systemic: it comes from vasodilation and whole-body inflammation, and the brain itself has no sensory receptors. Redness, swelling and drainage at the incision are local signs; they point to the site of infection.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2000. Both blood cultures show gram-negative rods (pink on Gram stain). Why does this result concern the team?
options: Gram-negative bacteria are the ones most receptive to antibiotics, so the drug choice hardly matters
A pink Gram stain shows these organisms are fungi, so the antibiotic won't work
An extra layer helps gram-negative bacteria evade both the immune system and antibiotics
Gram-negative bacteria cause local infection only and rarely reach the blood
questions.rationale: Gram-negative bacteria have an extra layer in the cell wall that helps them evade the immune system and antibiotics: "the armored tanks of the bacterial world… anytime you have gram-negative, it's not a good sign." Septicemia is usually caused by gram-negative bacteria. Gram-positive bacteria are the ones more receptive to antibiotics, and the Gram stain is used for bacteria, not fungi.

questions.stem: Day 1, 2300. T 39.6°C · HR 124 · BP 86/50. The immune system is now attacking and killing large numbers of the bacteria. The fever and falling blood pressure are best explained by:
options: A type I reaction, with IgE releasing histamine from mast cells
Colonization of the wound by normal skin flora that cause no damage
Exotoxins released steadily by the bacteria as they keep growing
Endotoxin (LPS) released as the gram-negative bacteria are lysed
questions.rationale: Endotoxins are the LPS of gram-negative bacteria and are released when the bacteria are attacked and lysed ("endo" = inside). They are pyrogenic, activate the inflammatory response and increase vascular permeability. In sepsis "it's your immune system going nuts," releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines that drop blood pressure. Exotoxins are released constantly during growth; type I is IgE-mediated allergy; colonization causes no damage.

questions.stem: The nurse anticipates the plan of care. Which items belong in it? Select all that apply.
options: Prepare for drainage of the wound abscess
Prepare for debridement of the infected tissue
Perform hand hygiene before and after all wound care
Request an antifungal in place of the antibiotic
Hold the antibiotic so the client builds natural immunity
Follow up on the wound and blood culture results
questions.rationale: A culture grows the organism outside the host to identify it. Slide 20's surgical interventions are draining abscesses, debridement and removing infected tissue; they are used when antibiotics can't reach bacteria protected by a thick biofilm. Hand washing is the nurse's core infection-control tool. "Natural immunity" means you always run the risk of dying, and antifungals don't treat bacteria.

questions.stem: Day 2, 1000. The lab reports that the organism makes an enzyme that inactivates the antibiotic the client is receiving. What should the nurse do?
options: Add an antihistamine to block the enzyme's effects
Keep giving the drug exactly as ordered, because the enzyme only matters in the lab dish
Double the next dose on her own to overpower the enzyme
Report the result to the provider promptly, since the current drug may not work
questions.rationale: Slide 17: one way bacteria "fight back" is by inactivating the antibiotic (others are altering its binding site, using different metabolic pathways and changing the cell wall to keep it out). A result like this means the drug may fail, so the provider needs it promptly. The nurse doesn't change a dose on her own, and antihistamines only block histamine receptors.

questions.stem: Day 4, 0800. The abscess was drained on Day 2 and the antibiotic was changed. Which findings show the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: BP 84/50 after his morning walk
Less drainage from the incision, and the redness is shrinking
New fluctuant swelling at the upper end of the incision
Says the muscle aches are gone and he walked the hall twice
questions.rationale: Fever and the systemic signs are resolving, vital signs are back to normal and the local signs are shrinking: he is moving toward convalescence and resolution. A new low blood pressure or a new fluctuant pocket (a possible new abscess) needs follow-up, not reassurance.

clinical.title: Scenario 2 — Pediatric clinic
clinical.setting: Pertussis exposure in a household · days 1–12
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1000 6-week-old infant brought in by the mother for a weight check. The father has had a cough for 2 weeks and today was diagnosed with pertussis at urgent care. He was vaccinated against pertussis as a teenager. The mother is up to date on her vaccines. The infant is exclusively breastfed and has not yet received any pertussis vaccine. A 4-year-old sibling has never been vaccinated. The infant has a mild runny nose and is feeding well. Vital Signs — Infant: T 37.0°C · HR 140 · RR 38 · SpO₂ 99% · weight up 30 g/day since birth Orders — Teach household infection-control measures · follow-up visit in 1 week

questions.stem: Which findings increase the infant's risk of whooping cough? Select all that apply.
options: Unvaccinated 4-year-old sibling in the home
Father with pertussis who lives in the home
Infant is exclusively breastfed
Mother is up to date on her vaccines
Infant T 37.0°C
Infant has not received any pertussis vaccine
questions.rationale: Pertussis spreads very easily (slide 3), and the infant has no vaccine protection and lives with a case plus an unvaccinated child who can catch and pass it on. Breast milk antibodies and a vaccinated mother are protective, not risks, and a normal temperature is just a normal finding.

questions.stem: The father says, "I don't understand. I was vaccinated, so how did I get whooping cough and give it to my family?" Which explanation is accurate?
options: Vaccinated adults can't spread pertussis, so the family got it somewhere else
The vaccine is against the toxin, not the bacteria, so the bacteria can still grow and spread
The pertussis vaccine only protects for a few days after it's given
His vaccine trained T cells to attack the bacteria themselves, but they missed this new strain
questions.rationale: The pertussis vaccine "is not actually for the bacteria. It's actually for a toxin the bacteria make." A vaccinated person can carry growing bacteria, do fine, and pass them to someone unvaccinated, who then makes the toxin and gets whooping cough. That's why high vaccination rates are needed. Tetanus is another anti-toxin vaccine.

questions.stem: The mother asks how her 6-week-old is protected, since the baby can't make much of an immune response yet. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The infant's T and B cell repertoire is already fully developed and diverse by 2 weeks after birth
The infant is protected by natural immunity, which lasts until about the first birthday
Newborns are born with a complete set of memory T and B cells copied from the mother
Breast milk antibodies reach the baby's blood, since the baby's stomach isn't very acidic yet
questions.rationale: The first step in fighting infection, developing a population of T and B cells, only starts after birth and takes time. Until then, breast milk antibodies help ("infants really don't have really acidic stomachs yet"), and the parents should be vaccinated. Newborns don't have memory cells, and the repertoire isn't diverse yet.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the household how to reduce spread to the infant. Which measures should be included? Select all that apply.
options: A face mask for the father around the family
Stopping breastfeeding to protect the infant
Skipping the sibling's vaccines until the outbreak is over
Letting the infant get pertussis to build natural immunity
Keeping the coughing father apart from the infant (isolation)
Hand washing before handling the infant
questions.rationale: The hygiene measures on slide 16 are hand washing, face masks, social distancing, quarantine and isolation: "stop it before it starts." Breastfeeding passes protective antibodies, so stopping it removes protection. "Natural immunity" carries the risk of dying, and vaccination rates are what protect babies who are too young for the vaccine.

questions.stem: Day 12, 0900. The infant is admitted with severe coughing spells. Which action should the nurse take first to protect others on the unit?
options: Place the infant on isolation and use the infection-control measures
Wait for the culture result before taking any precautions
Ask the parents to stop visiting the infant until the day of discharge home
Give the infant a pertussis vaccine dose to stop the toxin now
questions.rationale: Isolation is one of the infection-control measures on slide 16, and nurses use them so the disease never reaches the next person. Waiting for a result lets it spread in the meantime, and banning parents isn't on the list. A vaccine works by setting up a response over time, so it doesn't neutralize toxin that is already there.

questions.stem: Before discharge, which statements by the parents show they understood the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: "Getting sick is the best way for kids to build immunity."
"Our 4-year-old doesn't need vaccines because the baby will be immune."
"High vaccination rates help protect babies who are too young for the vaccine."
"My vaccine works against the toxin, so I could still carry the bacteria."
"Since I'm vaccinated, I can't spread it to anyone."
"Breastfeeding gives the baby some antibodies."
questions.rationale: These match his points: the vaccine targets the toxin, so carriers spread the bacteria and high vaccination rates are needed (the Northwest outbreak happened "because nobody understood how it actually worked"); breast milk passes antibodies. Vaccinated carriers can spread pertussis, "natural immunity" risks death, and the sibling's own vaccination is part of protecting the baby.

clinical.title: Scenario 3 — Employee health clinic
clinical.setting: mRNA vaccine, then an exposure · weeks 0–3
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 0, 0800 34-year-old client (a hospital unit clerk) received an mRNA COVID vaccine in the left deltoid. Observed 15 minutes with no problems. Takes loratadine (Claritin) daily for seasonal allergies. Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1600 (phone call) The client reports fever, muscle aches, fatigue and a headache since this morning, plus a tender, pea-sized lump in the left armpit. Breathing comfortably; no hives, no throat tightness. Sore at the injection site. Vital Signs — Day 1 (self-reported): T 38.1°C · HR 92 Orders — Employee-health vaccine teaching · follow-up as needed

questions.stem: Which of the client's Day 1 findings fit the expected response described in the vaccination deck? Select all that apply.
options: Fatigue and headache
Tender lump in the left armpit
Muscle aches
Age 34
Fever 38.1°C
Takes loratadine daily
questions.rationale: V-slide 5: the innate inflammatory/immune response causes the side effects seen 24–48 hours after vaccination: lethargy, myalgia, fever, headache. V-slide 6: APCs travel to the closest lymph node, which for a shoulder shot is "most likely the lymph node located in the arm pit," where proliferating cells make it swell. Her loratadine and her age aren't part of the vaccine response.

questions.stem: The client asks why her armpit is swollen. Put these events in the order they happened after the injection.
options: APCs carry the Spike2 antigen to the closest lymph node, in the armpit
Muscle cells take up the mRNA and release Spike2 while innate cells respond to the mRNA
APCs such as dendritic cells and macrophages present Spike2 on MHC II
A T cell whose receptor fits binds the APC's MHC II/Spike2 and divides by clonal proliferation
questions.rationale: V-slides 4–8: the innate system attacks the very immunogenic mRNA while muscle cells make and release Spike2 → APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages) phagocytose it and present it on MHC II → APCs travel to the closest node (armpit) → a matching T cell binds and clonally proliferates. The proliferation is what makes the node swell.

questions.stem: The client asks, "Does this fever mean the vaccine gave me COVID?" The client is most likely experiencing:
options: An early COVID infection caused by live virus in the vaccine
An expected innate inflammatory response to the vaccine
Serum sickness from circulating immune complexes
A type I allergic reaction to the mRNA in the vaccine
questions.rationale: mRNA is very immunogenic: it riles up innate immune cells, and that inflammatory/immune response causes lethargy, myalgia, fever and headache 24–48 hours later (V-slide 5). There is no virus in the vaccine to infect her. An allergy would show as hives, itching or airway signs, and she has none. Serum sickness is a type III reaction to foreign serum such as antivenom.

questions.stem: Which points should the nurse include in the client's teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Plasma cells keep producing antibodies against Spike2 for a time
The T cells released after the shot find no infection, so many expire and memory cells remain
The whole process of making memory cells takes about 10–14 days
She is fully protected within 24 hours of the shot
A later booster causes a secondary response, so antibody levels rise within days
The T cells released after the shot will attack her muscle cells
questions.rationale: V-slides 9–12: the released T cells and antibodies find no infection; activated cells have an "expiration date," memory T/B cells form and antibody production continues, over 10–14 days. Boosters cause a secondary response, with levels up within days (slide 52). Protection isn't immediate, and the T cells don't attack her own tissue.

questions.stem: Week 3. Eighteen days after her vaccination, the client had close contact with a coworker who now has COVID. She feels well. What should the nurse tell her?
options: She should double her daily loratadine to block the virus from entering her cells
She can't carry or spread COVID now that she's vaccinated, so no precautions are needed
She may spread it even without symptoms, so she should keep masking and washing hands
She should get a booster today to stop an infection that may already be starting
questions.rationale: V-slide 13: if a large viral load gets past the antibodies, infection starts with no signs or symptoms yet, "though the person may still spread COVID," and she may be contagious for a little while. Infection-control measures (masks, hand washing) limit spread. A booster sets up a secondary response; it doesn't stop an infection already underway. Antihistamines only block histamine receptors.

questions.stem: Which statements by the client show she understood the teaching about the exposure? Select all that apply.
options: "If it gets in, my memory T cells can find it and respond quickly."
"Even if I get sick, it's more likely to be mild than to put me in the hospital."
"My protection started the moment I got the shot."
"I can't catch or spread COVID anymore."
"If I get any symptoms at all, it means the vaccine failed."
"My antibodies may stop the virus before it gets into my cells."
questions.rationale: V-slide 13: antibodies bind Spike2 and effector cells and complement destroy the virus before it infects cells; if it gets in, memory T cells find it, proliferate and recruit help; minor symptoms can happen, but the person recovers instead of being hospitalized or dying. Spread is still possible for a short time, symptoms don't mean failure, and the process takes 10–14 days.

clinical.title: Scenario 4 — Primary care clinic
clinical.setting: Heel infection with a swollen node · days 1–10
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1100 58-year-old client with type 2 diabetes stepped on a shell at the beach 5 days ago. The right heel wound is red, warm, swollen and painful. Palpation finds a tender, enlarged lymph node behind the right knee; nodes in both groins are not enlarged. Scaly, itchy skin between the toes of both feet (the client calls it athlete's foot). Works as a mail carrier. Vital Signs — T 38.0°C · HR 94 · BP 134/82 · RR 16 Laboratory Results — Fingerstick glucose 238 mg/dL · wound culture: sent Orders — Oral antibiotic · topical antifungal to the toe webs · recheck in 10 days

questions.stem: Which findings show the client's immune system is responding to the heel infection? Select all that apply.
options: Groin nodes not enlarged
Tender, enlarged node behind the right knee
Red, warm, swollen heel
Temperature 38.0°C
Scaly skin between the toes
Works as a mail carrier
questions.rationale: A swollen node means T and B cells are proliferating there, and it is the node closest to the infection. Fever is a systemic sign, and redness, warmth and swelling are local signs at the site. The toe-web scaling is a separate (fungal) problem, normal groin nodes simply aren't involved, and his job is context.

questions.stem: The client asks why his toes need a different medicine than his heel. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Athlete's foot (tinea pedis) is a superficial fungal infection
Antibiotics will not kill fungi
Antifungals target ergosterol in the fungal membrane or glucan in the fungal wall
Tinea pedis is caused by a virus
Fungi are prokaryotes, like bacteria
The antibiotic also treats the fungus, so the cream is just extra
questions.rationale: Slide 12: dermatophytes invade skin, hair and nails, causing tineas (tinea pedis = feet); the fungal wall is made of different polysaccharides from bacterial peptidoglycan, so "antibiotics will not kill fungi." Slide 19: antifungals inhibit ergosterol and glucan. Fungi are eukaryotes, not prokaryotes.

questions.stem: The provider notes the client's diabetes. Why is this client at higher risk of a severe or spreading infection?
options: Diabetes is one of the illnesses that cause an acquired (secondary) immunodeficiency
Diabetes causes a type I reaction to bacteria
Diabetes is a primary (congenital) immunodeficiency caused by a single gene defect
Diabetes stops new T cells from being properly selected in the thymus, so none reach the nodes
questions.rationale: Diabetes is on the slide's list of acquired (secondary) causes: the immune system itself is fine, but another illness impairs it. The hallmark of an immune deficiency is multiple, severe infections. Primary deficiencies are congenital, usually single-gene defects.

questions.stem: Which items should the nurse include in the plan for the next 10 days? Select all that apply.
options: Palpate the node behind the knee at the recheck
Teach the client to apply the antifungal to the toe webs as ordered
Teach that an enlarged node means the infection has spread to the bloodstream
Hold the antibiotic so the client develops natural immunity
Apply the antifungal cream to the heel wound instead of taking the antibiotic
Follow up on the wound culture result
questions.rationale: Palpating nodes is how the nurse checks the proliferation he described, a culture identifies the organism, and the fungus needs the antifungal. Holding the antibiotic risks a severe infection, an antifungal doesn't treat bacteria, and a swollen node means the immune system is working at the closest node, not that the infection is in the blood.

questions.stem: The client asks how his body is fighting the heel infection. The nurse explains the steps. Put them in order.
options: APCs at the heel present the bacterial antigen on MHC II
APCs travel to the closest lymph node, behind the knee
A matching T cell binds the APC, then T cells proliferate and leave the node
Innate immune cells attack the bacteria in the heel and cause inflammation
questions.rationale: His step-by-step: infection → the innate system fights first ("could be the final step") → if there is a lot of inflammation, APCs present the antigen on MHC II → APCs travel to the closest lymph tissue → the right T cell binds → clonal proliferation, and the T cells leave. Step one, having the T and B cells in place, happened long before the injury.

questions.stem: Day 10, 1100. Which findings show the plan is working? Select all that apply.
options: Redness around the heel is shrinking
Less itching and scaling between the toes
Fingerstick glucose 251 mg/dL
A new fluctuant pocket of pus at the heel
The node behind the knee is smaller and no longer tender
questions.rationale: Fever is gone, the node is going down as the cells stop proliferating, the local heel signs are fading and the fungal skin is improving. A new pocket of pus suggests an abscess that may need draining (slide 20), and persistently high glucose keeps his diabetes-related risk going. Both need follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 5 — Emergency department
clinical.setting: Second bee sting in a breastfeeding client · 3 hours
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1430 29-year-old client stung on the forearm by a bee 20 minutes ago at a picnic. Last summer she was stung once and had only a small local bump. Now: hives on the arms and chest, intense itching, runny nose, red watery eyes and one episode of vomiting. Speaking in full sentences; no wheezing. She is breastfeeding a 4-month-old and plans to drive home. Vital Signs — T 36.9°C · HR 104 · BP 116/72 · RR 20 · SpO₂ 98% on room air Orders — Diphenhydramine IV once · monitor vital signs every 15 min

questions.stem: Which findings are signs of a type I (histamine-driven) reaction? Select all that apply.
options: Intense itching
Vomiting
Hives on the arms and chest
Speaking in full sentences
SpO₂ 98% on room air
Runny nose with red, watery eyes
questions.rationale: Slide 57's type I symptoms: GI (diarrhea, vomiting), skin (urticaria, pruritus), mucosa (conjunctivitis, rhinitis), airway (bronchoconstriction, mucus, edema) and vascular (angioedema, hypotension), with histamine as the main chemical. A normal SpO₂ and full sentences are reassuring findings, not signs of the reaction.

questions.stem: The client says, "I've been stung before and was fine. Why now?" Which explanation is accurate?
options: The first sting built tolerance, which has now worn off over the past year
Last summer's sting sensitized her immune system to the venom
Bee allergies only start in adulthood, usually after about age 25
This bee injected much more venom than the bee that stung her last summer
questions.rationale: "You can only have an immune reaction to something that your immune system has seen." The first sting sensitized her: T and B cells took 7–14 days, by which time the venom was long gone, so there was no reaction. Mast cells were primed, and this sting causes degranulation. Each sting raises the risk, so tolerance didn't build.

questions.stem: The nurse monitors the client. Which new findings would signal progression to anaphylaxis and need immediate action? Select all that apply.
options: Itching that is still present
SpO₂ dropping to 90%
Eyes still red and watery
BP falling to 84/50
New wheezing with throat tightness
More hives spreading to the back
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is the systemic, life-threatening form: mediators cause bronchoconstriction → hypoxia, and vasodilation → shock. "A very serious medical emergency." More hives, itching and watery eyes are still local/atopic signs of the same type I reaction.

questions.stem: Before giving the ordered diphenhydramine, which client factors should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
options: Her SpO₂ is 98%
Her first sting caused only a local bump
She is 29 years old
She plans to drive herself home
She is breastfeeding a 4-month-old
questions.rationale: Antihistamines are contraindicated in nursing mothers (sedation, decreased milk production; slide 64), and diphenhydramine is a highly sedating first-generation drug, so driving home afterward is a safety problem. Her age, normal SpO₂ and history of a mild first sting don't affect the drug decision.

questions.stem: What should the nurse do about the diphenhydramine order?
options: Give it, then tell her to breastfeed right away so the infant gets the dose
Hold it and clarify the order with the provider
Give it by mouth instead of IV so less reaches the milk
Give it now — antihistamines increase milk production
questions.rationale: Slide 64 lists nursing mothers as a contraindication, not a caution: antihistamines cause sedation and decrease milk production. He repeated it: "contraindicated in anybody nursing." The nurse holds the drug and clarifies with the provider. Changing the route doesn't remove a contraindication.

questions.stem: Day 1, 1730. Which findings show the client is improving? Select all that apply.
options: A new hoarse voice and throat tightness
Says, "Next time I'm stung I'll probably be fine."
Hives are fading
Itching is much less
SpO₂ 98% with no wheezing
questions.rationale: Fading skin signs with normal, stable vital signs and a clear airway show improvement. New hoarseness and throat tightness point to airway involvement (bronchoconstriction, edema) and need immediate follow-up. Her statement shows a gap in understanding: every sting increases the chance of a reaction.

clinical.title: Scenario 6 — Neurology clinic → emergency department
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Month 0, 0930 36-year-old client reports a drooping right eyelid and arm weakness when brushing her hair. Her mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Takes cetirizine (Zyrtec) for seasonal allergies. Walks her dog daily. Vital Signs — T 36.8°C · HR 76 · BP 118/74 · RR 14 · SpO₂ 99% Laboratory Results — Acetylcholine-receptor antibodies: positive Orders — Pyridostigmine PO · corticosteroid PO · neurology follow-up

questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with myasthenia gravis? Select all that apply.
options: SpO₂ 99%
Positive acetylcholine-receptor antibodies
Arm weakness when brushing her hair
Walks her dog daily
Drooping right eyelid
Takes cetirizine for seasonal allergies
questions.rationale: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies bind ACh receptors on muscle, so ACh can't activate the muscle → flaccid muscles, even paralysis; "the eyelid is flaccid." The positive antibody test fits. Her antihistamine, a normal SpO₂ and her daily walk aren't part of the picture.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes what is happening at the client's neuromuscular junction?
options: IgE on mast cells releases histamine that paralyzes the muscle
Antibodies block the ACh receptors like antagonists — a type II reaction
Sensitized T cells attack the muscle over 24–72 hours — type IV
Immune complexes deposit in the joints and kidneys — a type III reaction
questions.rationale: Myasthenia gravis is the slides' example of type II "target cell malfunction": antibodies bind receptors "kind of like antagonists, and block their activation." The antibodies are IgG/IgM against a specific tissue (self), so it's autoimmune. IgE/histamine is type I, circulating complexes are type III, and T cells are type IV.

questions.stem: Month 4, 2100. The client is brought to the ED with severe generalized weakness, trouble swallowing and shallow breathing. SpO₂ 91%. The client is most likely experiencing:
options: Serum sickness
Sedation from a second-generation antihistamine
Anaphylaxis from her cetirizine
A myasthenic crisis
questions.rationale: Worsening blockade of ACh receptors → muscle weakness up to paralysis; slide 68 names this the myasthenic crisis. Anaphylaxis is a type I reaction with hives, bronchoconstriction and shock; cetirizine is a second-generation drug with much less sedation, which wouldn't explain profound weakness.

questions.stem: Which treatments does the nurse anticipate for the crisis? Select all that apply.
options: IV immune globulin (IVIG)
A switch to diphenhydramine
Hydroxychloroquine
Rho(D) immune globulin IM
Plasma exchange
questions.rationale: Slide 68: "plasma exchange and intravenous immune globulin should be given in myasthenic crises." Plasma exchange cleans antibodies out of the blood. Rho(D) immune globulin is for Rh sensitization, hydroxychloroquine is on the SLE slide, and a sedating antihistamine has no role.

questions.stem: The client's partner asks what plasma exchange does. Which explanation is accurate?
options: It replaces her own T cells with matched donor T cells from a blood bank
It adds extra acetylcholine to her blood so more reaches the muscle
It cleans the antibodies that block her receptors out of the blood
It removes her thymus, where the faulty cells were selected
questions.rationale: "You can clean out the blood of any antibodies via plasma exchange." More ACh comes from an AChE inhibitor (pyridostigmine) that stops its breakdown, and the thymus is removed by thymectomy, a separate surgery.

questions.stem: Month 6. The client is stable and her thymectomy is scheduled. Which statements show she understands her treatment? Select all that apply.
options: "The thymus surgery is because too many of the wrong cells got through selection."
"The steroid calms down my immune system's overreaction."
"This is an allergy to my own acetylcholine, like a bee-sting allergy."
"Pyridostigmine keeps more acetylcholine around by slowing its breakdown."
"Pyridostigmine removes the antibodies from my blood."
questions.rationale: His treatment logic: increase ACh by stopping its breakdown (pyridostigmine), corticosteroids "to decrease the immune overreaction," and thymectomy "if you think it's due to too many cells getting through the selection process." Removing antibodies is plasma exchange, and myasthenia gravis is type II autoimmunity, not a type I IgE allergy.

clinical.title: Scenario 7 — Emergency department → medical unit
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 1500 46-year-old client bitten on the left ankle by a rattlesnake while hiking. Received antivenom in the ED and was discharged on Day 3. Nurses' Notes — Day 10, 1100 Returns with fever, an itchy rash on the trunk, painful swollen knees and wrists, and tender swollen nodes in the neck and groin. The bite site is healing well. Urine is foamy. Vital Signs — T 38.4°C · HR 98 · BP 132/84 · RR 18 · SpO₂ 98% Laboratory Results — Urine protein: positive · creatinine: higher than at discharge Orders — Admit · strict intake and output · daily kidney labs

questions.stem: Which Day 10 findings fit the slide's description of serum sickness? Select all that apply.
options: Fever 38.4°C
Tender swollen lymph nodes
SpO₂ 98%
Rash on the trunk
Bite site healing well
Painful swollen knees and wrists
questions.rationale: Slide 69: serum sickness (with antivenom as the example) causes fever, enlarged lymph nodes, rash, pain and arthritis. A healing bite site and a normal SpO₂ aren't part of it.

questions.stem: Which mechanism explains the client's illness?
options: Antibody–antivenom complexes circulating and lodging in tissues
IgE on mast cells reacting to venom still left in the tissues
Sensitized T cells reaching the joints after 24–72 hours
Antibodies binding to the cells of a single organ, such as the kidney
questions.rationale: Type III: free antigen (here, the foreign serum proteins in antivenom) + antibody → circulating immune complexes, "giant roaming balls," that get stuck in blood vessels, joints and kidneys, activate complement and damage tissue. It is not organ-specific. Organ-specific antibody binding is type II, IgE is type I, and T cells are type IV.

questions.stem: Which finding is the nurse's highest priority to report and follow?
options: The itchy rash spreading across the trunk and back
Temperature of 38.4°C
The tender, swollen lymph nodes in the neck and groin
The positive urine protein with a rising creatinine
questions.rationale: Kidneys are one of the three sites most affected by immune complexes (with vessels and joints), and glomerulonephritis is on the slide's list of systemic type III diseases. Protein in the urine with a rising creatinine means organ damage is happening. Fever, rash and swollen nodes are expected features of serum sickness.

questions.stem: Which items does the nurse anticipate in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Record the reaction to antivenom in the client's history
Arrange a crossmatch for a transplant
Give Rho(D) immune globulin IM
Trend the daily kidney labs
Assess the swollen joints and rash each shift
Measure intake and output strictly
questions.rationale: Kidneys, joints and vessels are where the complexes lodge, so the nurse tracks kidney function, joints and skin. Documenting the reaction tells future teams the client has had serum sickness from antivenom. A crossmatch is for transplants, and Rho(D) immune globulin is for Rh-negative mothers.

questions.stem: The client asks, "Am I allergic to rattlesnake venom now?" Which response is accurate?
options: "Yes, this is an IgE allergy to the venom itself, just like a bee-sting allergy."
"Your T cells are attacking the bite site and joints, which takes 24–72 hours."
"The snake's toxin is still circulating in your bloodstream, and that's what is causing all of this."
"Your antibodies bound the antivenom proteins into complexes that lodged in tissues."
questions.rationale: Serum sickness is a side effect of the treatment: "the antivenom antibodies in there can start forming these giant complexes and getting stuck in places" (type III). It isn't an IgE allergy to venom (type I) or a T-cell reaction (type IV).

questions.stem: Day 14, 0800. Which findings show the client is improving? Select all that apply.
options: Urine output 60 mL/h, urine no longer foamy
Knee and wrist swelling has gone down
Urine protein still strongly positive and rising
New purple, non-blanching spots on both legs
Creatinine back down toward the discharge value
questions.rationale: Fever, arthritis and the kidney findings are all resolving. Rising urine protein means continued kidney damage, and new skin lesions could mean vessel involvement (vasculitis is on the slide's list of systemic type III diseases), so both need follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 8 — Rheumatology clinic
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Month 0, 1000 27-year-old client with 6 weeks of painful, swollen finger joints and knees, a rash across the cheeks and fatigue. Had strep throat 2 months ago. Her older sister has lupus. Works as a dental hygienist. Up to date on vaccines. Vital Signs — T 37.6°C · HR 88 · BP 126/80 · RR 16 Laboratory Results — Hemoglobin: low (anemia) · urine protein: positive · antibodies to nuclear material (histones, nucleic acids): positive Orders — Hydroxychloroquine · glucocorticoid · NSAID as needed for joint pain · recheck in 3 months

questions.stem: Which findings fit the multisystem picture of SLE? Select all that apply.
options: Up to date on vaccines
Low hemoglobin (anemia)
Painful, swollen joints
Works as a dental hygienist
Rash across the cheeks
Protein in the urine
questions.rationale: Slide 74: SLE is a chronic multisystem inflammatory disease: arthritis, vasculitis and rash, renal disease, hematologic abnormalities (especially anemia) and cardiovascular disease. Her job and vaccination status are background, not SLE findings.

questions.stem: Which parts of her history fit the causes of autoimmunity he wants you to know? Select all that apply.
options: A sister with lupus
Works as a dental hygienist
Up to date on vaccines
Strep throat 2 months ago
Female sex
questions.rationale: "Know that it's either genetic predisposition, breakdown of tolerance or molecular mimicry." Genetic predisposition: autoimmunity is more common in women, and her sister has lupus. His SLE story: during a strep throat, an APC may present a histone that's floating around and find a T or B cell for it → autoimmunity. Her job and vaccines aren't on the list.

questions.stem: Which best describes how SLE damages her kidneys and joints?
options: Antibodies block one receptor on a single organ, like the kidney — type II
IgE-coated mast cells release histamine into the joints and kidneys — type I
Autoantibodies form circulating complexes that lodge in tissues — type III
Sensitized T cells attack the kidney and joints over 24–72 hours — type IV
questions.rationale: Slide 74: SLE produces autoantibodies against nucleic acids, histones and other nuclear material, and "circulating immune complexes form: type III." They clog vessels, joints and kidneys. Single-receptor blockade is type II (myasthenia gravis), and T-cell attack is type IV.

questions.stem: Which medications does the nurse expect for SLE, based on the slide? Select all that apply.
options: Diphenhydramine
Glucocorticoids (corticosteroids)
Hydroxychloroquine
NSAIDs
Rho(D) immune globulin
Pyridostigmine
questions.rationale: Slide 74 lists immunosuppressives for SLE: hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids/corticosteroids and NSAIDs. Pyridostigmine is for myasthenia gravis, Rho(D) immune globulin is for Rh sensitization, and antihistamines don't touch the immune response.

questions.stem: Month 3. The joint pain and rash have settled. The client asks, "Does this mean I'm cured?" Which response is best?
options: "Yes. You can stop all of your medicines now that the symptoms are gone."
"No, and it will steadily get worse from here no matter which medicines you take."
"Yes. Once the rash and joint pain are gone, lupus doesn't come back."
"Lupus usually goes through remissions and flares, so keep your follow-up visits."
questions.rationale: Remissions and exacerbations are common to autoimmune diseases (slide 74); SLE is chronic, so a quiet period isn't a cure. Neither "cured" nor "steadily worse" fits the pattern on the slide.

questions.stem: At the 3-month visit, which findings show the treatment is working? Select all that apply.
options: Finger and knee swelling has gone down
New chest pain when lying flat
Urine protein is now higher than at diagnosis
Hemoglobin is rising toward normal
The cheek rash is fading
Urine protein is negative
questions.rationale: Arthritis, rash, anemia and kidney findings are all improving. New chest pain could be the cardiovascular involvement on the slide's list, and rising urine protein means more kidney damage, so both need follow-up.

clinical.title: Scenario 9 — Labor & delivery → postpartum unit
clinical.setting: Rh-negative mother with a postpartum hemorrhage · days 1–2
clinical.text: Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0610 31-year-old client delivered her first baby vaginally after an epidural. Mother's blood type: O, Rh-negative. Father: Rh-positive. Newborn: Rh-positive, Apgar 8 and 9, breastfeeding well. Nurses' Notes — Day 1, 0745 Heavy vaginal bleeding; the fundus is boggy. Vital Signs — 0745: HR 122 · BP 88/54 · RR 22 · SpO₂ 97% Laboratory Results — Hemoglobin falling · type and crossmatch: in progress Orders — Transfuse packed red blood cells when crossmatched · Rho(D) immune globulin IM before discharge

questions.stem: Which findings are relevant to the risk of Rh alloimmunity? Select all that apply.
options: Newborn's Apgar scores 8 and 9
Newborn is Rh-positive
Newborn is breastfeeding well
Mother received an epidural
Mother is Rh-negative
Father is Rh-positive
questions.rationale: Slide 78's example is an Rh-negative mother with an Rh-positive father and child. The epidural, the Apgar scores and how well the baby is feeding have nothing to do with Rh sensitization.

questions.stem: The client asks whether her newborn is in danger from the Rh difference. Which explanation is accurate?
options: The baby can be harmed only if she breastfeeds while Rh-negative
There is no risk now or in any future pregnancy, because the father is Rh-positive
This baby faces the greatest danger because it is her first pregnancy
This baby is usually fine; a future Rh-positive baby is the one at risk
questions.rationale: "The first birth, fine. Because remember, there wasn't a sensitizing event." Birth exposes her to the baby's blood and is the sensitizing event; the problem comes with the next Rh-positive pregnancy (erythroblastosis fetalis/hemolytic disease of the newborn). This is type II alloimmunity.

questions.stem: Day 1, 0810. The client needs red blood cells. She is type O. Which ABO type of red cells is compatible with her?
options: Type AB, because AB is the universal type that works for anyone
Any ABO type, since only Rh matters in pregnancy
Type A, because it is the most common type
Type O, because she makes antibodies against both A and B
questions.rationale: Type O expresses neither A nor B antigen, so an O person has antibodies against both and can receive only O. O is the universal donor; AB is the universal recipient, not the universal donor. Giving another type causes a transfusion reaction (type II alloimmunity).

questions.stem: Which items does the nurse anticipate in the plan for the transfusion and the Rh risk? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm the crossmatch before hanging the blood
Give Rho(D) immune globulin by the IM route as ordered
Watch for a transfusion reaction during the infusion
Give AB red cells if crossmatching is delayed
Give the Rho(D) immune globulin to the newborn instead
questions.rationale: Mismatched blood triggers a transfusion reaction (slide 77), so the crossmatch is confirmed and the client is watched during the transfusion. Slide 78: Rho(D) immune globulin (RhoGAM, Rhophylac, MICRhoGAM) is given IM. AB is the universal recipient, so AB cells would trigger a reaction in a type O client, and the slide doesn't describe giving the drug to the baby.

questions.stem: Day 2, 0900. The nurse prepares the ordered Rho(D) immune globulin. By which route is it given?
options: Subcutaneous injection
Slow IV push
Intramuscular injection
Oral tablet
questions.rationale: Slide 78 lists Rho(D) immune globulin (Rhophylac, RhoGAM, MICRhoGAM) and "IM"; he repeated, "It's an intramuscular shot."

questions.stem: Before discharge, which statements show the client understands the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: "If I'm sensitized, my next Rh-positive baby is the one at risk."
"AB blood would have been the safest choice for me."
"I got type O blood because O has neither A nor B antigen."
"Giving birth can expose my immune system to the baby's Rh-positive blood."
"This baby is at highest risk because it's my first."
questions.rationale: Birth is the sensitizing event, the risk is to a later Rh-positive baby, and O cells carry neither A nor B, so they're safe for a type O recipient. AB is the universal recipient, so AB cells would cause a reaction in her, and the first baby is usually fine.

clinical.title: Scenario 10 — Rapid rounds
clinical.setting: Transplant unit, clinic and ED · one question each
clinical.text: Six clients, one question each. Read each stem on its own.

questions.stem: Before a kidney transplant, donor and recipient blood are mixed and the recipient's antibodies lyse the donor cells. What should the nurse expect?
options: The test is repeated after an antihistamine
The transplant goes ahead, with extra immunosuppressants added to prevent acute rejection
The transplant goes ahead, since lysis only predicts chronic rejection
The transplant is canceled, since this result predicts hyperacute (type II) rejection
questions.rationale: Crossmatching: "take the blood of the donor and blood of the recipient, mix it… If there's any cell lysis, that means it's incompatible, and we definitely do not do the transplant." Otherwise the graft would suffer hyperacute rejection: immediate, type II, from preexisting antibodies. Acute and chronic rejection are type IV.

questions.stem: Three weeks after a bone marrow transplant, a client develops a rash and diarrhea, and the team suspects the graft is attacking the client. Why is this possible?
options: The donor marrow carries anti-A and anti-B antibodies into the blood
The recipient's preexisting antibodies are destroying the donor marrow
The graft triggers an IgE (type I) reaction in the skin and the gut
Bone marrow makes immune cells, so the donor's cells can attack the host
questions.rationale: Graft-versus-host disease (type IV): "bone marrow is where immune cells come from," so the transplanted immune component attacks host tissues that carry antigens foreign to it. Recipient antibodies destroying a graft describes hyperacute rejection (the opposite direction).

questions.stem: A nurse places a TB skin test on a new employee. The employee asks why the result isn't checked right away. The nurse explains that:
options: Antibodies need a few minutes to bind the test antigen in the skin
Sensitized T cells must travel to the site, which takes 24–72 hours
Mast cells need about a week to release enough histamine
The test site must first be swabbed and cultured in the lab
questions.rationale: The TB skin test is a type IV (cell-mediated) reaction: if you've had TB, T cells travel to that part of the skin, activate and proliferate. That takes time, 24–72 hours on slide 71. Reactions driven by antibodies (types I–III) are immediate.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client has been taking diphenhydramine (Benadryl) nightly for sleep. Which effects should the nurse assess for? Select all that apply.
options: New confusion
Urinary retention
Falls or near-falls
Increased milk production
Blurred vision
Diarrhea
questions.rationale: Older adults are on the caution list (slide 64): serious anticholinergic effects such as confusion, sedation, constipation, blurred vision and urinary retention, plus more falls and a possible link to dementia. First-generation diphenhydramine is highly sedating. Its GI effect is constipation, not diarrhea, and decreased (not increased) milk is the nursing-mother concern.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old swallowed several of a grandparent's antihistamine tablets. Which findings fit antihistamine toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Flushed face
Pinpoint pupils
CNS excitation (agitation)
Tachycardia
Heavy drooling
Dilated pupils
questions.rationale: Slide 63: CNS and anticholinergic toxicity cause dilated pupils, flushed face, hyperpyrexia, tachycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention, and children show CNS excitation (very young children are especially sensitive to CNS stimulation). The pupils are dilated, not pinpoint, and the mouth is dry rather than drooling. Acute toxicity is rare because of the large margin of safety, but the drugs are everywhere.

questions.stem: Which clients have an acquired (secondary) immunodeficiency? Select all that apply.
options: An infant with SCID
A child with C3 deficiency
A client with alcoholic cirrhosis
A client with AIDS
A client with severe malnutrition
A client who is 30 weeks pregnant
questions.rationale: Acquired deficiencies are caused by another condition: pregnancy (immunity naturally suppressed to protect the baby), AIDS, alcoholic cirrhosis (decreased complement) and malnutrition are all on slide 82. SCID and C3 deficiency are primary (congenital/genetic) defects.
