qa.q: Can anybody give me an example of a disease where the immune system attacks something the organism makes, not the organism? Has anybody heard of whooping cough?
qa.a: Pertussis. The bacteria make a toxin that causes the cough; the vaccine is against the toxin, so the immune system neutralizes it while the bacteria are still there.

qa.q: (student asked) Can you spread COVID before you have symptoms?
qa.a: Yes: some diseases spread while you're asymptomatic. For rabies, the animal has to be showing signs to pass it on.

qa.q: Do you think the extra layer makes gram-negative bacteria more or less destructive than gram-positive?
qa.a: More: the extra layer evades the immune system and antibiotics. "These are like the armored tanks of the bacterial world."

qa.q: (student asked) Which color is which on a Gram stain?
qa.a: "Pink is negative, purple is positive."

qa.q: Why would fever, headache and myalgia be considered systemic, not local?
qa.a: Student: the headache has nothing to do with the brain. Accepted: it comes from vasodilation and whole-body inflammation; the brain has no sensory receptors.

qa.q: (Kahoot) True or false: all interactions between humans and microorganisms are detrimental.
qa.a: False: we have good bacteria in the gut and on the skin, and the best way to keep bad bacteria out is to have good ones take up the space.

qa.q: (Kahoot) True or false: certain bacterial cells release proteins called endotoxins during growth.
qa.a: False: those are exotoxins. Endotoxins are inside the bacteria and released only when they are attacked.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which pathogen is an intracellular parasite consisting of a protein coat surrounding a nucleic acid?
qa.a: The answer wasn't audible. Virus (from slide 7).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which type of infection is treated based on the results of a Gram stain?
qa.a: Bacterial.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Put pathogenicity in order.
qa.a: Communicability → infectivity → virulence (audio garbled; order from slide 3).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Put the disease course in order.
qa.a: Incubation → prodromal → acute → convalescent → resolution.

qa.q: (Kahoot) True or false: signs and symptoms show up in the subclinical phase.
qa.a: False: little to no signs or symptoms. A scratchy throat isn't really a sign.

qa.q: You guys know what humors are?
qa.a: His explanation was garbled. The point: humoral immunity = antibodies secreted into the bloodstream.

qa.q: Why does adaptive immunity take a while? Are these antibodies specific or non-specific?
qa.a: Very specific: one antibody binds one antigen, so each has to be made by its own cell.

qa.q: Do you know how many proteins our DNA actually makes?
qa.a: He said "5,000, 10,000"; slide 28 says 26,000 protein-coding genes, far too few for 10¹² receptors. That's the diversity problem.

qa.q: Is DNA very protected? What happens to a cell with DNA damage?
qa.a: It dies. Immune cells are different: they purposely rearrange their DNA to make many different antibodies.

qa.q: Do you think every rearranged cell will make a useful antibody? Should a useless cell stay alive?
qa.a: No: "this is all hitting the lottery." A useless cell is a waste of resources, so it's told to die (positive selection).

qa.q: Say an immune cell really likes to bind neurons. Good thing or bad thing?
qa.a: Bad: it would attack you (autoimmunity), so it's removed by negative selection.

qa.q: Why is just one cell per antigen stored in a lymph node, and not 1,000 copies?
qa.a: With 10¹² different kinds, making copies of each means you'd run out of space.

qa.q: When that one cell divides on infection, what do we call it?
qa.a: Clonal proliferation.

qa.q: Can anybody give me a clinical example of when T cells and B cells divide, something you do to patients?
qa.a: Palpating lymph nodes. Swollen = T/B cells dividing: good (immune system working) and bad (active infection). The closest node responds: foot infection → behind the knee.

qa.q: What is the very first thing that needs to happen to fight infection?
qa.a: Develop a population of T and B cells, before the infection even happens. "Students always get this wrong."

qa.q: Why aren't infants constantly dying of infection, before vaccination?
qa.a: Breast milk: its antibodies can reach the bloodstream because infant stomachs aren't very acidic yet. Parents should be vaccinated too.

qa.q: After vaccination, when the T cells are released, do they attack anything?
qa.a: No: there's no active infection. They eventually die but leave a bigger population for a faster secondary response.

qa.q: (student asked) Are these cells stored in the bone marrow, or do they live in the lymph node?
qa.a: B cells are selected in the bone marrow and T cells in the thymus; both then go to the lymph nodes.

qa.q: (student asked) Why does vaccine efficacy differ between diseases?
qa.a: Incubation and mutation: measles takes about a week to 10 days and rarely mutates, so the vaccine prevents illness. COVID (3–4 days) and flu are quick, so trials measured hospitalization and death, not "not getting sick."

qa.q: (student asked) What about sepsis?
qa.a: Sepsis is your immune system going nuts: pro-inflammatory cytokines, a drop in blood pressure. Unvaccinated COVID deaths were the same "haywire" response, treated with corticosteroids.

qa.q: If someone is vaccinated against pertussis, can they still spread the disease? Why?
qa.a: Yes: the vaccine is against the toxin, not the bacteria, so carriers spread it. We need high vaccination rates (Northwest outbreak). Tetanus is also an anti-toxin vaccine.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Which immune cells create antibodies and respond to antigens?
qa.a: B cells (B lymphocytes; "lymphocytes" and "T/B cells" are used interchangeably).

qa.q: (Kahoot) Innate or adaptive: specific immunity?
qa.a: Adaptive.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Innate or adaptive: neutrophils, skin, antibodies, "quick," lymph nodes?
qa.a: Neutrophils innate · skin innate · antibodies adaptive · quick innate · lymph nodes adaptive (audio partly garbled).

qa.q: (Kahoot, multi-select) Macrophages: innate or adaptive?
qa.a: Both: innate cells that the adaptive system tells where to kill.

qa.q: (Kahoot) Positive and negative selection are also called…?
qa.a: Tolerance.

qa.q: If you've never been stung by a bee, can you be allergic to a bee sting? (show of hands)
qa.a: No: you can only react to something your immune system has seen. The first sting is the sensitizing event.

qa.q: After the first sting, when the T and B cells leave the lymph node, will they see the bee venom? How long does that take?
qa.a: No: it takes 7–14 days and the venom is long gone. A sting a month later may cause a reaction.

qa.q: What is the problem with this APC [in peanut allergy]?
qa.a: It found a T cell specific for peanuts that should have been selected out. The gut normally surveys food and builds tolerance.

qa.q: Kids with dogs, or who spend time on a farm, are less likely to develop allergies. Why?
qa.a: Constant, diverse exposure gets to the thymus so positive and negative selection happen correctly.

qa.q: What's anaphylaxis?
qa.a: You can't breathe (airway constriction) and you get too much vasodilation, leading to shock: "a very serious medical emergency."

qa.q: (student asked) I'm allergic to shellfish, though my mother ate plenty while pregnant. How did that happen?
qa.a: Likely an APC presented shellfish protein during a gut infection to a T cell that fit only ~80%: "it's not a perfect system" (this leads into molecular mimicry).

qa.q: A child gets a local reaction at the site of a vaccine shot. Why is this happening?
qa.a: Student: the child was already exposed. Accepted: B cells were ready, and antibodies met the concentrated antigen at the injection site → complexes (Arthus reaction).

qa.q: Have you guys ever had a TB skin test?
qa.a: It's type IV: if you've had TB, sensitized T cells travel to that patch of skin, activate and proliferate. That takes time (slide 71: 24–72 h).

qa.q: (student asked) Do antibodies cross the placenta?
qa.a: "I think immunoglobulins do pass over [the] placenta." (slide 26 table: IgG crosses)

qa.q: What are the rejections?
qa.a: Hyperacute (type II; crossmatch catches it) and acute and chronic (type IV). Most people develop some, so immunosuppressants are for life; identical twins are the exception.

qa.q: Bone marrow transplant: why can the donor's cells attack the recipient?
qa.a: Bone marrow is where immune cells come from, so the graft attacks the host: graft-versus-host disease.
